## Summer 2026 Pre-Assignment

**Part 1: R Basics for Development Data**

**Estimated time:** 1.5-3 hours

This assignment introduces the basic R habits you will use in the rest of the
summer work: running code, creating objects, using functions, checking logical
statements, and reading simple error messages. The examples use development
data concepts because API-209 and the MPA/ID curriculum use data to reason
carefully about policy questions.

## Why knit?

Knitting runs this whole document from top to bottom in a fresh R session. This
checks whether your work is reproducible: the code, output, and written answers
can be rebuilt in order. Running chunks manually is useful while learning, but a
successful knit is the best check that your assignment is complete and
self-contained.

## Project folders

The project has a stable structure:

```text
summer-assignments/
  assignments/
  data/
  figs/
  scripts/
```

You are working in the `assignments/` folder. Later assignments will load data
from `../data/development_indicators_2026.csv`. The `..` means "go up one
folder," so `../data/` points from `assignments/` to the shared data folder.

## Data types

R works with different kinds of values. Numbers are numeric values. Words inside
quotation marks are character values.

```{r}
2026
"Harvard Kennedy School"
"Ghana"
```

Write your name as a character value:

```{r}
# Write your name below, inside quotation marks.
```

## Logical values

Logical values are `TRUE` or `FALSE`. They are central to filtering data later.
The operator `==` asks whether two things are equal.

```{r}
3 == 3
2 == 4
"Ghana" == "Kenya"
```

The operator `!=` asks whether two things are not equal.

```{r}
"Ghana" != "Kenya"
2024 != 2023
```

## Objects

Objects store values so you can use them later. The assignment operator `<-`
puts the value on the right into the name on the left.

```{r}
country <- "Ghana"
year <- 2023
population <- 33787914
```

Run the object names to see what they store:

```{r}
country
year
population
```

You can use objects in calculations.

```{r}
population_millions <- population / 1000000
population_millions
```

You can also use objects in logical checks.

```{r}
country == "Ghana"
year >= 2020
```

## Functions

Functions perform tasks. Most functions use parentheses.

```{r}
sqrt(9)
log(100)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

The values inside parentheses are called arguments. Some arguments are required;
others are optional.

```{r}
mean(c(10, 20, 30))
max(c(10, 20, 30))
min(c(10, 20, 30))
```

## Vectors

A vector stores several values in one object. Use `c()` to combine values.

```{r}
peer_countries <- c("Ghana", "Kenya", "Rwanda", "Tanzania")
growth_rates <- c(3.8, 5.6, 8.2, 5.1)
```

Run the objects:

```{r}
peer_countries
growth_rates
mean(growth_rates)
growth_rates > 5
```
